title: Henderson at Red Banks
summary: Henderson began at Red Banks, named for red clay on the Ohio River shore, and took its name from Richard Henderson of the Transylvania Company.
bodyMarkdown:
[Henderson](https://grokipedia.com/page/Henderson,_Kentucky) began at a place called Red Banks, named for the red clay exposed along the Ohio River shore, where records show a community by 1784. Native peoples had long used the area for hunting and travel along the river, though there were [no permanent Native villages](https://grokipedia.com/page/Henderson,_Kentucky) there by the late 1700s. That early community was made up mostly of short-term squatters.

## A grant born of a failed colony

The town's name goes back to [Richard Henderson](/stories/richard-henderson/), a North Carolina judge and land speculator. In 1775 his [Transylvania Company](https://grokipedia.com/page/Transylvania_Colony) bought a vast tract from the Cherokee at Sycamore Shoals. Cherokee leaders including Oconostota and Attakullakulla signed, but the purchase broke British and colonial rules against private land buys from Native nations.

Virginia voided the purchase. According to the [City of Henderson's history](https://hendersonky.gov/141/History-of-Henderson), Virginia then granted Richard Henderson and Company 200,000 acres in 1778, in recognition of the $50,000 the company had paid the Cherokee. Land from that grant lies within today's Henderson County. Richard Henderson died in 1785, before his town was laid out.

## Laying out the town

The first documented permanent settlement came in 1791, upstream from Red Banks, on Henderson Company land. General Samuel Hopkins, a Revolutionary War officer acting as the company's agent, and surveyor Thomas Allin laid out the town of Henderson. They finished the plan on April 6, 1797, and the city still counts that as its birth date.

Henderson County was formed from Christian County in December 1798 and organized on June 4, 1799, with the renamed Red Banks as its seat. The town was incorporated in 1810 with 183 residents. The city's history notes that the Ohio and Mississippi rivers gave local farms access to markets through New Orleans.

## Audubon's years

The naturalist [John James Audubon](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_James_Audubon) moved to Henderson in 1810 and lived there until 1819. In 1816 he and his brother-in-law Thomas Bakewell built a steam-powered saw and grist mill on the Ohio River. The mill had mechanical problems from the start and collapsed in the Panic of 1819. Audubon drew inspiration from Henderson's wildlife, and his later bird studies made him famous.

## Kentucky today

Henderson sits across the river from Evansville, Indiana, and is part of the Evansville–Henderson combined statistical area. [Audubon State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_James_Audubon_State_Park) and its museum honor the naturalist's years in town. The plan completed on April 6, 1797, set the grid of Henderson's core on the bluff that once gave Red Banks its name.
